title: Recognising risk signals and making a referral
audience: Consultants who may meet clients whose descriptions of eating, weight, exercise or health suggest that a referral is needed before any general habit support continues.
learningOutcomes: Describe the kinds of client statements that call for a pause and a referral.
Respond to a client who discloses distress about food, weight or body in a neutral, non-judgmental way.
Follow the referral and escalation route without diagnosing the client.
Record a concern and the action taken, using the client's own words where appropriate.

instruction.heading: Why this lesson is different
instruction.body: A general habit consult can be the first place where a client talks about a problem with food, weight or body image. The practitioner is not a clinician and must not diagnose. The practitioner is responsible for noticing when a conversation has moved beyond general support, for pausing the work and for referring the client to someone who can assess them. This lesson describes how to respond. It does not provide a screening tool, and it does not tell you whether a client has any condition. The list of signals below is a working guide only. The qualified reviewer, who should be a clinician with eating-disorder experience, must confirm, change or replace it before the course is published. Its content is UNCONFIRMED in this draft.

instruction.heading: Kinds of statements that call for a pause
instruction.body: Statements that call for a pause include a client describing eating in secret, strict rules that they feel unable to break, guilt or fear after eating, self-induced vomiting or laxative or diuretic use, compulsive or punishing exercise, a sudden or unexplained change in weight they report, fainting or dizziness they report, a request to be told how to lose weight quickly and a sense of hopelessness about their body. Pregnancy, a current medication, a diagnosed condition, a child or young person, and a history of an eating disorder are also referral situations, as set out in the first lesson. The list is a working guide. It is not a checklist to score, and one statement does not prove a condition. Your task is to notice, pause and refer.

instruction.heading: Responding to a disclosure
instruction.body: When a client discloses distress, stay calm and listen. Thank them for telling you. Use neutral language that does not blame food or the client. Do not argue with how the client feels about their body, and do not say that their concern is not serious. Do not promise that the problem can be fixed by changing the diet. Say that a health professional can help them understand what they are experiencing, and that you want them to get that support. Ask what support they already have, if that feels right to them, and do not press for detail they have not offered. Do not diagnose, and do not name a condition unless a health professional has done so.

instruction.heading: Making the referral
instruction.body: Pause the general consult. Tell the client that you will not continue the habit plan until they have spoken with a suitable health professional, and explain the reason in plain words. Give the referral route that the business has confirmed, such as a general practitioner or another registered health professional, and encourage the client to make contact. Do not give a diagnosis, a diet or a supplement in place of the referral. If the client asks what to do next, point to the referral route and to the business's escalation contact. Where a client describes an immediate danger to their health or safety, follow the emergency procedure in the business's safety plan and contact emergency services without delay.

instruction.heading: Recording and escalating a concern
instruction.body: Record the date, what the client said in their own words where appropriate, what you said in reply, the action you took and the referral made. Keep the note factual and avoid labels such as the name of any condition. Escalate to the business owner and the qualified reviewer any concern you are not sure how to handle, any case that involves a child or a person at immediate risk, and any repeated concern across sessions. The referral route, the escalation contacts and the wording of the referral letter are not confirmed in this draft and must be supplied by the business and checked by the reviewer.

instruction.heading: Verification and escalation
instruction.body: A supervisor or the qualified reviewer should check the referral route and the escalation contacts before any client is seen. A competent practitioner can name the statements that call for a pause, respond to a disclosure without judgment, pause and refer without diagnosing, and record the concern and the action. Escalate immediately where a client is at risk of harm. Do not attempt to resolve a risk situation alone.

procedure: Listen for statements that suggest distress, unsafe eating or exercise, a referral situation or a change in health.
Pause the general consult and keep the response calm and neutral.
Do not diagnose, do not name a condition and do not offer a plan to resolve the concern.
Explain the referral route in plain words and give the confirmed contact details.
Where there is immediate risk, follow the emergency procedure and contact emergency services without delay.
Record the disclosure, the response, the referral and the time, and escalate to the owner and the reviewer as the policy requires.

workedExamples.situation: A client says they have been skipping meals for weeks, feel very guilty after eating and have started exercising for two hours a day to make up for it.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What do you do in this session?
workedExamples.reasoning: This is a referral situation. Pause the habit plan, respond calmly and without judgment, and do not give a meal plan or a restriction target. Explain that you want them to speak with a suitable health professional before you go further, and give the confirmed referral route. Record the statements in the client's words, your response and the referral. Escalate to the owner and the reviewer under the policy.

workedExamples.situation: A client who has just been discharged from a hospital stay says they want to lose weight quickly before a family event, and asks for the fastest method.
workedExamples.reasoning: Do not offer a fast method, a target or a timeline. A recent hospital stay and a request for fast change are both reasons to pause and refer. Tell the client that you cannot advise on a fast approach and that they should check with their treating health professional first. Record the request and the referral.

equipmentAndPpe: Confirmed referral route and contact list for the business
Escalation contact list, including the qualified reviewer and business owner
Client record system with the approved note template

commonErrors.error: Diagnosing the client or naming a condition because the signs look familiar.
commonErrors.prevention: Describe what the client said and refer them. The diagnosis belongs to a health professional.

commonErrors.error: Responding to a disclosure with criticism of the client's eating or appearance.
commonErrors.prevention: Respond calmly and neutrally, and focus on connecting the client with support.

commonErrors.error: Continuing the habit plan because the client asks you to, and the plan seems harmless.
commonErrors.prevention: Pause the plan when a referral situation appears and refer, whatever the client asks.

commonErrors.error: Dealing with a risk situation alone and not escalating it.
commonErrors.prevention: Follow the emergency procedure where there is immediate risk, and escalate to the owner and reviewer for any concern you are not sure about.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Eating-disorder screening is not provided in this lesson. The screening approach, and whether a general consultant may use any screening at all, is an open question that must be answered by the qualified reviewer. The lesson does not resolve it.
Where there is immediate risk to a client's health or safety, follow the business's emergency procedure and contact emergency services. This takes priority over any habit plan.
Completing this lesson does not give authority to assess, diagnose or treat any eating or medical condition.

qualityStandard: The practitioner paused the general consult when a referral situation appeared, and did not continue a plan for that client in that session.
No diagnosis, condition label, diet target or supplement was offered in response to a disclosure.
The referral was given with the confirmed route, and the client was encouraged to make contact.
The disclosure, the response, the referral and any escalation were recorded factually.
documentationEvidence: Session note with the date, the client's statements in their own words where appropriate, the response and the referral.
Record of any escalation to the owner or reviewer, with the date and the person informed.
Record of any emergency procedure followed, where it applied.
summary: Notice statements that suggest distress, unsafe eating or exercise, or a referral situation, and pause the general consult.
Respond calmly and without judgment, and do not diagnose or offer a plan to resolve the concern.
Refer through the confirmed route and record the disclosure, the response and the referral.
Escalate immediately where there is risk, and to the reviewer for any concern you are not sure about.

knowledgeChecks.question: A client describes strict rules about food, guilt after eating and exercise to make up for it. What is the first action?
options: Pause the habit plan, respond calmly and refer the client to a suitable health professional.
Write a stricter plan with a clear target so the client feels in control
Name the condition the client seems to have so they can look it up

knowledgeChecks.question: Which response to a disclosure is best?
options: Tell the client that their concern is not serious and to focus on their diet
Thank the client for telling you, respond neutrally and help them connect with support.
Criticise the client's eating so they understand the problem

knowledgeChecks.question: A client describes an immediate danger to their health. What takes priority?
options: Finishing the habit plan so the session can close on time
Following the emergency procedure and contacting emergency services without delay.
Booking another session to discuss the matter later in the week
